concepts: Orthocentre, centroid and circumcentre of a triangle (Euler line) in vector form
questions.question: Let the position vectors of three vertices of a triangle be $4\vec p+\vec q-3\vec r$, $-5\vec p+\vec q+2\vec r$ and $2\vec p-\vec q+2\vec r$. If the position vectors of the orthocentre and the circumcentre of the triangle are $\frac{\vec p+\vec q+\vec r}{4}$ and $\alpha\vec p+\beta\vec q+\gamma\vec r$ respectively, then $\alpha+2\beta+5\gamma$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The orthocentre $H$, centroid $G$ and circumcentre $C$ are collinear with $HG:GC=2:1$, so $G=\frac{H+2C}{3}$.
solution: The centroid is $G=\frac{(4\vec p+\vec q-3\vec r)+(-5\vec p+\vec q+2\vec r)+(2\vec p-\vec q+2\vec r)}{3}=\frac{\vec p+\vec q+\vec r}{3}$.
The orthocentre $O$, centroid $G$ and circumcentre $C$ lie on a line (the Euler line) with $OG:GC=2:1$.
By the section formula, $G=\frac{1\cdot O+2\cdot C}{3}$, i.e. $\frac{\vec p+\vec q+\vec r}{3}=\frac{\frac{\vec p+\vec q+\vec r}{4}+2(\alpha\vec p+\beta\vec q+\gamma\vec r)}{3}$.
So $2(\alpha\vec p+\beta\vec q+\gamma\vec r)+\frac{\vec p+\vec q+\vec r}{4}=\vec p+\vec q+\vec r$.
Comparing the coefficients of $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ (taken as linearly independent): $2\alpha+\frac14=1$, so $\alpha=\frac38$.
In the same way $\beta=\gamma=\frac38$.
Hence $\alpha+2\beta+5\gamma=8\cdot\frac38=3$, which is option (2).
useful_results: Euler line: $H$, $G$, $C$ are collinear with $G$ dividing $HC$ internally in the ratio $2:1$, so $\vec g=\frac{\vec h+2\vec o}{3}$ with $\vec o$ the circumcentre; since $3\vec g=\vec a+\vec b+\vec c$ for vertices $A,B,C$, this is $\vec h=\vec a+\vec b+\vec c-2\vec o$.
With the circumcentre as origin ($\vec o=\vec 0$), $\vec h=\vec a+\vec b+\vec c$ (Sylvester's relation): the orthocentre is the sum of the vertex vectors.
If a vector equation holds with $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ non-coplanar, coefficients can be compared one by one; no dot products of $\vec p,\vec q,\vec r$ are needed.
Here the vertex sum is $\vec p+\vec q+\vec r$, so $\vec o=\frac12\left(\vec p+\vec q+\vec r-\vec h\right)=\frac38(\vec p+\vec q+\vec r)$.

concepts: Vector product and projection of a vector
questions.question: Let $\vec a=3\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k$, $\vec b=\vec a\times(\hat i-2\hat k)$ and $\vec c=\vec b\times\hat k$. Then the projection of $\vec c-2\hat j$ on $\vec a$ is:
questions.key_idea: Compute the two cross products by determinants, then use projection $=\frac{(\vec c-2\hat j)\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|}$.
solution: $\vec b=\vec a\times(\hat i-2\hat k)=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\3&-1&2\\1&0&-2\end{matrix}\right|=2\hat i+8\hat j+\hat k$.
$\vec c=\vec b\times\hat k=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&8&1\\0&0&1\end{matrix}\right|=8\hat i-2\hat j$.
So $\vec c-2\hat j=8\hat i-4\hat j$.
Projection of $\vec c-2\hat j$ on $\vec a$ is $\frac{(8\hat i-4\hat j)\cdot(3\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k)}{\sqrt{9+1+4}}$.
$=\frac{24+4}{\sqrt{14}}=\frac{28}{\sqrt{14}}=2\sqrt{14}$, which is option (3).

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand $(\vec a\times\vec m)\times\hat k$ with the vector triple product formula instead of two determinants.
solution: Put $\vec m=\hat i-2\hat k$, so $\vec b=\vec a\times\vec m$ and $\vec c=(\vec a\times\vec m)\times\hat k$.
Use $(\vec u\times\vec v)\times\vec w=\vec v(\vec u\cdot\vec w)-\vec u(\vec v\cdot\vec w)$: $\vec c=\vec m(\vec a\cdot\hat k)-\vec a(\vec m\cdot\hat k)$.
$\vec a\cdot\hat k=2$ and $\vec m\cdot\hat k=-2$, so $\vec c=2(\hat i-2\hat k)+2(3\hat i-\hat j+2\hat k)=8\hat i-2\hat j$.
Then $\vec c-2\hat j=8\hat i-4\hat j$ and its projection on $\vec a$ is $\frac{24+4}{\sqrt{14}}=2\sqrt{14}$.

useful_results: Vector triple product: $(\vec u\times\vec v)\times\vec w=\vec v(\vec u\cdot\vec w)-\vec u(\vec v\cdot\vec w)$ (the middle vector gets the positive sign); $\vec u\times(\vec v\times\vec w)=\vec v(\vec u\cdot\vec w)-\vec w(\vec u\cdot\vec v)$.
Scalar projection of $\vec x$ on $\vec a$ is $\frac{\vec x\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|}$ (signed); the vector projection is $\frac{\vec x\cdot\vec a}{|\vec a|^2}\vec a$.
Crossing with a coordinate unit vector is quick: $(x,y,z)\times\hat k=(y,-x,0)$, which gives $(2,8,1)\times\hat k=(8,-2,0)$ here.

concepts: Angle bisector of two vectors and distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let $A,B,C$ be three points in the $xy$-plane whose position vectors with respect to the origin $O$ are $\sqrt3\hat i+\hat j$, $\hat i+\sqrt3\hat j$ and $a\hat i+(1-a)\hat j$ respectively. If the distance of the point $C$ from the line bisecting the angle between the vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$ is $\frac{9}{\sqrt2}$, then the sum of all the possible values of $a$ is:
questions.key_idea: The bisector of $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$ is along $\hat a+\hat b$, here the direction $\hat i+\hat j$; then use distance $=|\vec r\times\hat d|$.
solution: The angle bisector of $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$ is along $\widehat{OA}+\widehat{OB}$.
$\widehat{OA}+\widehat{OB}=\frac{\sqrt3\hat i+\hat j}{2}+\frac{\hat i+\sqrt3\hat j}{2}=\frac{(\sqrt3+1)}{2}(\hat i+\hat j)$.
So the bisector is the line through $O$ with direction $\vec d=\hat i+\hat j$: $\vec r=\vec 0+\lambda(\hat i+\hat j)$.
Distance of $C$ from this line is $\frac{|\overrightarrow{OC}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}=\frac{|(a\hat i+(1-a)\hat j)\times(\hat i+\hat j)|}{\sqrt2}=\frac{9}{\sqrt2}$.
$(a\hat i+(1-a)\hat j)\times(\hat i+\hat j)=(a-(1-a))\hat k=(2a-1)\hat k$, so $|2a-1|=9$.
Sum of the possible values $=5+(-4)=1$, which is option (2).

alternate_solutions.idea: $|OA|=|OB|=2$, so $A$ and $B$ are mirror images in the line $y=x$, which is therefore the bisector; use the point-to-line distance formula.
solution: $|OA|=|OB|=2$ and $B$ is $A$ with its coordinates swapped, so $A,B$ are reflections of each other in $y=x$.
The bisector of the angle $AOB$ is therefore the line $y=x$, i.e. $x-y=0$.
The distance of $C(a,1-a)$ from $x-y=0$ is $\frac{|a-(1-a)|}{\sqrt2}=\frac{|2a-1|}{\sqrt2}$.
Setting $\frac{|2a-1|}{\sqrt2}=\frac{9}{\sqrt2}$ gives $|2a-1|=9$, so $a=5$ or $a=-4$, with sum $1$.

useful_results: The internal bisector of the angle between $\vec u$ and $\vec v$ is along $\hat u+\hat v$ (equivalently $\frac{\vec u}{|\vec u|}+\frac{\vec v}{|\vec v|}$); when $|\vec u|=|\vec v|$ it is along $\vec u+\vec v$ (the diagonal of a rhombus).
Distance of a point with position vector $\vec p$ from the line $\vec r=\vec a+\lambda\vec d$ is $\frac{|(\vec p-\vec a)\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$.
Points $(x,y)$ and $(y,x)$ are mirror images in $y=x$; a vector pair of equal length that are such mirror images has bisector $y=x$.

concepts: Resolution of a vector into components parallel and perpendicular to another vector
questions.question: If the components of $\vec a=\alpha\hat i+\beta\hat j+\gamma\hat k$ along and perpendicular to $\vec b=3\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$ respectively are $\frac{16}{11}\left(3\hat i+\hat j-\hat k\right)$ and $\frac{1}{11}\left(-4\hat i-5\hat j-17\hat k\right)$, then $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec a$ is the sum of its component along $\vec b$ and its component perpendicular to $\vec b$, so $\vec a$ can be read off directly.
solution: Write $\vec a=\vec a_{\parallel b}+\vec a_{\perp b}$, where $\vec a_{\parallel b}=\left(\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|^2}\right)\vec b$ is the component along $\vec b$.

Given $\vec a_{\parallel b}=\frac{16}{11}(3\hat i+\hat j-\hat k)$ and $|\vec b|^2=9+1+1=11$, we get $\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{11}=\frac{16}{11}$, so $\vec a\cdot\vec b=16$, i.e. $3\alpha+\beta-\gamma=16$.

$\vec a_{\perp b}=\vec a-\vec a_{\parallel b}=\left(\alpha-\frac{48}{11}\right)\hat i+\left(\beta-\frac{16}{11}\right)\hat j+\left(\gamma+\frac{16}{11}\right)\hat k=\frac{-4}{11}\hat i-\frac5{11}\hat j-\frac{17}{11}\hat k$.
$\alpha-\frac{48}{11}=-\frac4{11}$ gives $\alpha=4$.
$\beta-\frac{16}{11}=-\frac5{11}$ gives $\beta=1$.
$\gamma+\frac{16}{11}=-\frac{17}{11}$ gives $\gamma=-3$.
$\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=16+1+9=26$, which is option (3).

alternate_solutions.idea: The two components are perpendicular, so by Pythagoras $|\vec a|^2=|\vec a_{\parallel}|^2+|\vec a_{\perp}|^2$; no need to find $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$.
solution: Since $\vec a_{\parallel b}\perp\vec a_{\perp b}$, we have $|\vec a|^2=|\vec a_{\parallel b}|^2+|\vec a_{\perp b}|^2$ and $|\vec a|^2=\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$.
$|\vec a_{\parallel b}|^2=\left(\frac{16}{11}\right)^2\cdot11=\frac{256}{11}$.
Sum $=\frac{256+30}{11}=\frac{286}{11}=26$, which is option (3).

useful_results: Component of $\vec a$ along $\vec b$ is $\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|^2}\vec b$; the perpendicular component is $\vec a-\frac{\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec b|^2}\vec b$, and the two are orthogonal.
Pythagoras for components: $|\vec a|^2=\frac{(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2}{|\vec b|^2}+|\vec a_{\perp b}|^2$ (equivalently $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$).
Check: the perpendicular component must satisfy $\vec a_{\perp}\cdot\vec b=0$; here $(-4,-5,-17)\cdot(3,1,-1)=-12-5+17=0$.

concepts: Cross product identities and magnitude of a vector
questions.question: Let $\vec a=2\hat i-\hat j+3\hat k$, $\vec b=3\hat i-5\hat j+\hat k$ and $\vec c$ be a vector such that $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec c\times\vec b$ and $(\vec a+\vec c)\cdot(\vec b+\vec c)=168$. Then the maximum value of $|\vec c|^2$ is:
questions.key_idea: $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec c\times\vec b$ gives $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=\vec 0$, so $\vec c$ is parallel to $\vec a+\vec b$.
solution: $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec c\times\vec b$ gives $\vec a\times\vec c+\vec b\times\vec c=\vec 0$, i.e. $(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=\vec 0$.
So $\vec c$ is parallel to $\vec a+\vec b$: $\vec c=\lambda(\vec a+\vec b)=\lambda(5\hat i-6\hat j+4\hat k)$.
$(\vec a+\vec c)\cdot(\vec b+\vec c)=\big((2+5\lambda)\hat i-(1+6\lambda)\hat j+(4\lambda+3)\hat k\big)\cdot\big((3+5\lambda)\hat i-(6\lambda+5)\hat j+(1+4\lambda)\hat k\big)=168$.
$(2+5\lambda)(3+5\lambda)+(1+6\lambda)(6\lambda+5)+(4\lambda+3)(1+4\lambda)=168$, which simplifies to $77\lambda^2+77\lambda+14=168$.
So $\lambda^2+\lambda-2=0$, i.e. $(\lambda+2)(\lambda-1)=0$ and $\lambda=-2$ or $\lambda=1$.
$|\vec c|^2=\lambda^2(25+36+16)=77\lambda^2$, which is $308$ for $\lambda=-2$ and $77$ for $\lambda=1$.
The maximum value of $|\vec c|^2$ is $308$, which is option (1).

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand $(\vec a+\vec c)\cdot(\vec b+\vec c)=\vec a\cdot\vec b+(\vec a+\vec b)\cdot\vec c+|\vec c|^2$ and use $\vec c=\lambda\vec s$ with $\vec s=\vec a+\vec b$, so only $\vec a\cdot\vec b$ and $|\vec s|^2$ are needed.
solution: As before $\vec c=\lambda\vec s$, with $\vec s=\vec a+\vec b=(5,-6,4)$ and $|\vec s|^2=77$.
$(\vec a+\vec c)\cdot(\vec b+\vec c)=\vec a\cdot\vec b+\vec c\cdot(\vec a+\vec b)+|\vec c|^2=\vec a\cdot\vec b+\lambda|\vec s|^2+\lambda^2|\vec s|^2$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec b=6+5+3=14$, so $14+77(\lambda+\lambda^2)=168$ and $\lambda^2+\lambda=2$.
$\lambda=1$ or $-2$; $|\vec c|^2=77\lambda^2\in\{77,308\}$, so the maximum is $308$.

useful_results: $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec c\times\vec b\iff(\vec a+\vec b)\times\vec c=\vec 0\iff\vec c\parallel(\vec a+\vec b)$ (or $\vec c=\vec 0$). Similarly $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec b\times\vec c$ gives $\vec c\parallel(\vec a-\vec b)$.
$(\vec x+\vec c)\cdot(\vec y+\vec c)=\vec x\cdot\vec y+(\vec x+\vec y)\cdot\vec c+|\vec c|^2$: expanding symbolically avoids component arithmetic.
When $\vec c=\lambda\vec s$, $|\vec c|^2=\lambda^2|\vec s|^2$; a quadratic in $\lambda$ gives two vectors, so a question asking for the 'maximum' compares both roots.

concepts: Line of shortest distance between two skew lines
questions.question: Let $L_1:\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-3}{4}$ and $L_2:\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-4}{4}=\frac{z-5}{5}$ be two lines. Then which of the following points lies on the line of the shortest distance between $L_1$ and $L_2$?
questions.key_idea: The line of shortest distance is $PQ$ with $P\in L_1$, $Q\in L_2$ and $PQ\perp$ both lines, which fixes $P$ and $Q$ by two linear equations.
solution: Take $P(2\lambda+1,\,3\lambda+2,\,4\lambda+3)$ on $L_1$ and $Q(3\mu+2,\,4\mu+4,\,5\mu+5)$ on $L_2$.
Direction ratios of $PQ$: $(3\mu-2\lambda+1,\ 4\mu-3\lambda+2,\ 5\mu-4\lambda+2)$.
Solving (1) and (2): $\lambda=\frac13$ and $\mu=-\frac16$.
So $P\left(\frac53,3,\frac{13}{3}\right)$ and $Q\left(\frac32,\frac{10}{3},\frac{25}{6}\right)$.
The line $PQ$ is $\frac{x-\frac53}{\frac16}=\frac{y-3}{-\frac13}=\frac{z-\frac{13}{3}}{\frac16}$, i.e. $\frac{x-\frac53}{1}=\frac{y-3}{-2}=\frac{z-\frac{13}{3}}{1}$.
For $\left(\frac{14}{3},-3,\frac{22}{3}\right)$: $x-\frac53=3$, $y-3=-6$, $z-\frac{13}{3}=3$, in the ratio $1:-2:1$, so it lies on $PQ$: option (4).

alternate_solutions.idea: The common perpendicular has direction $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$; it is the intersection of the plane through $L_1$ and that direction with the plane through $L_2$ and that direction. Test each option in both planes.
solution: $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=(2,3,4)\times(3,4,5)=(-1,2,-1)\parallel(1,-2,1)=\vec n$: this is the direction of the line of shortest distance.
Plane $\Pi_1$ through $L_1$ and parallel to $\vec n$: normal $=(2,3,4)\times(1,-2,1)=(11,2,-7)$, through $(1,2,3)$, so $11x+2y-7z+6=0$.
Plane $\Pi_2$ through $L_2$ and parallel to $\vec n$: normal $=(3,4,5)\times(1,-2,1)=(14,2,-10)\parallel(7,1,-5)$, through $(2,4,5)$, so $7x+y-5z+7=0$.
The line of shortest distance is $\Pi_1\cap\Pi_2$ (it lies in both planes because it meets each line and is parallel to $\vec n$).
For $\left(\frac{14}{3},-3,\frac{22}{3}\right)$: $\frac{154}{3}-6-\frac{154}{3}+6=0$ and $\frac{98}{3}-3-\frac{110}{3}+7=0$, so it lies on both planes.
Options (1), (2), (3) fail $\Pi_1$ (values $-\frac{100}{3},\,31,\,\frac{95}{3}$ for $11x+2y-7z+6$), so the answer is (4).

useful_results: Shortest distance between skew lines $\vec a_1+\lambda\vec d_1$, $\vec a_2+\mu\vec d_2$ is $\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)|}{|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|}$ and the common perpendicular has direction $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$.

The common perpendicular is the intersection of two planes: [plane through $L_1$ containing $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$] $\cap$ [plane through $L_2$ containing $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$]; membership of a given point is then a two-equation check.
Setting $PQ\perp L_1,L_2$ always gives two linear equations in the two parameters; their determinant is non-zero exactly when the lines are not parallel.
Here $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=(-1,2,-1)$ and $\vec PQ=\left(-\frac16,\frac13,-\frac16\right)$ are parallel, which is a quick check on $\lambda,\mu$.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular from a point on a line and area of a triangle
questions.question: Let in a $\triangle ABC$, the length of the side $AC$ be $6$, the vertex $B$ be $(1,2,3)$ and the vertices $A,C$ lie on the line $\frac{x-6}{3}=\frac{y-7}{2}=\frac{z-7}{-2}$. Then the area (in sq. units) of $\triangle ABC$ is:
questions.key_idea: The height from $B$ is the distance from $B$ to the line $AC$, i.e. $BM$ with $M$ the foot of the perpendicular.
solution: Let $M$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ on line $AC$: $M(3\lambda+6,\,2\lambda+7,\,-2\lambda+7)$.
$\overrightarrow{BM}=(3\lambda+5)\hat i+(2\lambda+5)\hat j+(-2\lambda+4)\hat k$.
$\overrightarrow{AC}\cdot\overrightarrow{BM}=0$: $3(3\lambda+5)+2(2\lambda+5)-2(-2\lambda+4)=0$, i.e. $17\lambda+17=0$, so $\lambda=-1$.
Then $\overrightarrow{BM}=2\hat i+3\hat j+6\hat k$ and $|\overrightarrow{BM}|=\sqrt{4+9+36}=7$.
Area $=\frac12\times AC\times BM=\frac12\times6\times7=21$, which is option (2).

alternate_solutions.idea: Height $=\frac{|\overrightarrow{BP_0}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$ for a point $P_0$ on the line, with no parameter to solve.
solution: A point on the line is $P_0(6,7,7)$ with direction $\vec d=(3,2,-2)$, $|\vec d|^2=17$.
$\overrightarrow{BP_0}=(5,5,4)$ and $\overrightarrow{BP_0}\times\vec d=(5\cdot(-2)-4\cdot2,\ 4\cdot3-5\cdot(-2),\ 5\cdot2-5\cdot3)=(-18,22,-5)$.
$|\overrightarrow{BP_0}\times\vec d|^2=324+484+25=833=49\cdot17$, so the height is $\frac{\sqrt{833}}{\sqrt{17}}=7$.
Area $=\frac12\cdot6\cdot7=21$.

useful_results: Distance of a point $B$ from the line through $P_0$ with direction $\vec d$ is $\frac{|\overrightarrow{P_0B}\times\vec d|}{|\vec d|}$.
Area of a triangle with base on a line is $\frac12\times$ base $\times$ (distance of the opposite vertex from that line); the position of $A,C$ on the line is irrelevant, only $AC$ matters.
The foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to the line $P_0+\lambda\vec d$ has $\lambda=\frac{\overrightarrow{P_0B}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$; here $\lambda=\frac{(-5,-5,-4)\cdot(3,2,-2)}{17}=-1$.

concepts: Equation of a line in 3D and point of intersection of two lines
questions.question: Let the line passing through the point $(-1,2,1)$ and parallel to the line $\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{3}=\frac z4$ intersect the line $\frac{x+2}{3}=\frac{y-3}{2}=\frac{z-4}{1}$ at the point $P$. Then the distance of $P$ from the point $Q(4,-5,1)$ is:
questions.key_idea: The required line is $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-1}{4}$; set it equal to the second line's parametrisation and solve for the common point.
solution: The line through $(-1,2,1)$ parallel to $(2,3,4)$ is $\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{3}=\frac{z-1}{4}=\lambda$, i.e. $x=2\lambda-1,\ y=3\lambda+2,\ z=4\lambda+1$.
The second line: $\frac{x+2}{3}=\frac{y-3}{2}=\frac{z-4}{1}=\mu$, i.e. $x=3\mu-2,\ y=2\mu+3,\ z=\mu+4$.
At the point of intersection $P$: $2\lambda-1=3\mu-2$, $3\lambda+2=2\mu+3$ and $4\lambda+1=\mu+4$.
From the first two equations $\lambda=1,\ \mu=1$ (and the third holds: $5=5$).

alternate_solutions.idea: A point of the second line lies on the required line exactly when $\overrightarrow{MP}\parallel(2,3,4)$, which uses only one unknown.
solution: Let $M(-1,2,1)$ and $P(3\mu-2,\,2\mu+3,\,\mu+4)$ on the second line.
$\overrightarrow{MP}=(3\mu-1,\ 2\mu+1,\ \mu+3)$ must be parallel to $(2,3,4)$.

useful_results: A line through $M$ with direction $\vec d$ meets a second line at $P$ iff $\overrightarrow{MP}\times\vec d=\vec 0$ for the corresponding point $P$ of the second line: one parameter instead of two.

Two lines meet iff they are coplanar and non-parallel: $(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec d_1\times\vec d_2)=0$. Here $(-2,3,4)-(-1,2,1)=(-1,1,3)$ is checked against $(2,3,4)\times(3,2,1)=(-5,10,-5)$: $5+10-15=0$.
The distance between points $(x_1,y_1,z_1),(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ is $\sqrt{\Sigma\Delta^2}$; $9+100+16=125=5^3$ gives $5\sqrt5$.

concepts: Circumcentre of a triangle in 3D (equidistant point) and nature and area of a triangle
questions.question:
Let $A(x,y,z)$ be a point in the $xy$-plane, which is equidistant from three points $(0,3,2)$, $(2,0,3)$ and $(0,0,1)$. Let $B=(1,4,-1)$ and $C=(2,0,-2)$. Then among the statements
(S1): $\triangle ABC$ is an isosceles right angled triangle, and
(S2): the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $\frac{9\sqrt2}{2}$:
questions.key_idea: Equidistance from three points gives two linear equations; with $z=0$ they fix $A=(3,2,0)$, after which the triangle's sides decide both statements.
solution: In the $xy$-plane $z=0$. From $AQ=AR$: $x^2-4x+4+y^2+9=x^2+y^2+1$, so $13-4x=1$ and $x=3$.
$AB=AC$ and $AB^2+AC^2=9+9=18=BC^2$, so $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles and right-angled at $A$: (S1) is true.
Area $=\frac12\times AB\times AC=\frac12\times3\times3=\frac92\ne\frac{9\sqrt2}{2}$, so (S2) is false.
Only (S1) is true: option (4).

alternate_solutions.idea: Equidistance from two points is a linear (perpendicular-bisector) equation; then check the right angle with a dot product and the area with a cross product.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}=(-2,2,-1)$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=(-1,-2,-2)$; $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=2-4+2=0$, so the angle at $A$ is $90^\circ$, and $|AB|=|AC|=3$: (S1) is true.
$\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}=(-6,-3,6)$ with magnitude $9$, so the area is $\frac92$, not $\frac{9\sqrt2}{2}$: (S2) is false.

useful_results: The set of points equidistant from $P$ and $Q$ is the plane $2\vec x\cdot(\vec Q-\vec P)=|\vec Q|^2-|\vec P|^2$; three such conditions are linear and give the circumcentre-type point without squares.
A triangle with sides $p,q,r$ is right-angled iff the squares add ($r^2=p^2+q^2$); equivalently two edge vectors have zero dot product.
Area $=\frac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$; for a right angle at $A$ this equals $\frac12|AB||AC|$, so the stated $\frac{9\sqrt2}{2}$ would need legs of product $9\sqrt2$, not $9$.

concepts: Line perpendicular to two given lines (common direction by cross product)
questions.question: Let $L_1:\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-1}=\frac{z-1}{2}$ and $L_2:\frac{x+1}{-1}=\frac{y-2}{2}=\frac z1$ be two lines. Let $L_3$ be a line passing through the point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ and be perpendicular to both $L_1$ and $L_2$. If $L_3$ intersects $L_1$, then $|5\alpha-11\beta-8\gamma|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $L_3$ has direction $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$, and $5\alpha-11\beta-8\gamma$ is constant because $(5,-11,-8)$ is normal to the plane of $L_1$ and $L_3$.
solution: $L_3$ is perpendicular to both, so its direction is $\vec d_3=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&-1&2\\-1&2&1\end{matrix}\right|=-5\hat i-3\hat j+\hat k$.
Let $L_3$ meet $L_1$ at $Q(1+\lambda,\,2-\lambda,\,1+2\lambda)$; then $\overrightarrow{PQ}=t(-5,-3,1)$ where $P=(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is the given point.
So $1+\lambda-\alpha=-5t$, $2-\lambda-\beta=-3t$, $1+2\lambda-\gamma=t$ .
Hence $\alpha=1+\lambda+5t$, $\beta=2-\lambda+3t$, $\gamma=1+2\lambda-t$.
$5\alpha-11\beta-8\gamma=(5-22-8)+(5\lambda+11\lambda-16\lambda)+(25t-33t+8t)=-25$, free of $\lambda$ and $t$.
So $|5\alpha-11\beta-8\gamma|=25$, which is option (2).
questions.correction_note: The PDF lists the three component equations and then jumps to '|5alpha-11beta-8gamma| = 25' with no working (the substitution that makes lambda and the multiplier cancel is missing). Added the substitution steps; the answer 25 is correct. The PDF's multiplier is called mu, which clashes with the parameter of L2.

alternate_solutions.idea: $(5,-11,-8)=\vec d_1\times\vec d_3$ is the normal of the plane containing the intersecting lines $L_1$ and $L_3$; that plane passes through $(1,2,1)$ on $L_1$.
solution: $L_3$ has direction $\vec d_3=(-5,-3,1)$ and $L_1$ has direction $\vec d_1=(1,-1,2)$.
$L_1$ and $L_3$ intersect, so they lie in one plane, with normal $(5,-11,-8)$.
That plane contains $(1,2,1)\in L_1$: $5x-11y-8z=5-22-8=-25$.
The point $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ is on $L_3$, hence on this plane: $5\alpha-11\beta-8\gamma=-25$ and the required value is $25$.

useful_results: Two intersecting lines with directions $\vec d_1,\vec d_3$ lie in the plane through either one with normal $\vec d_1\times\vec d_3$; any point of $L_3$ satisfies that plane's equation.
A coefficient triple that appears in the question (here $5,-11,-8$) is often a cross product of two direction vectors: compute $\vec d_1\times\vec d_3$ as a check.
A line perpendicular to two lines with directions $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ has direction $\vec d_1\times\vec d_2$; by itself it is not unique unless a point is given, but the plane of $L_1$ and $L_3$ is.

concepts: Foot of perpendicular from a point on a line and intersection of two lines
questions.question: Let $P$ be the foot of the perpendicular from the point $(1,2,2)$ on the line $L:\frac{x-1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{-1}=\frac{z-2}{2}$. Let the line $\vec r=(-\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k)+\lambda(\hat i-\hat j+\hat k)$, $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, intersect the line $L$ at $Q$. Then $2(PQ)^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $P$ and $Q$ both lie on $L$, so only their two parameter values on $L$ are needed: first the foot of the perpendicular, then the intersection.
solution: Let $A(1,2,2)$. A point of $L$ is $P(\mu+1,\,-\mu-1,\,2\mu+2)$, with direction $\vec d=(1,-1,2)$.
$\overrightarrow{AP}=(\mu,\,-\mu-3,\,2\mu)$ and $\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\vec d=0$: $\mu+\mu+3+4\mu=0$, so $\mu=-\frac12$.
$P=\left(\frac12,-\frac12,1\right)$.
The general point of the second line is $(-1+\lambda,\,1-\lambda,\,-2+\lambda)$; equate it with $(\mu+1,\,-\mu-1,\,2\mu+2)$.
$\mu+1=-1+\lambda$ gives $\mu=\lambda-2$; $-\mu-1=1-\lambda$ gives the same $\mu=\lambda-2$; $2\mu+2=-2+\lambda$ gives $2(\lambda-2)+2=-2+\lambda$, so $\lambda=0$.
$PQ=\sqrt{\left(\frac12+1\right)^2+\left(-\frac12-1\right)^2+(1+2)^2}=\sqrt{\frac94+\frac94+9}=\sqrt{\frac{54}{4}}$.
$2(PQ)^2=2\cdot\frac{54}{4}=27$, which is option (2).

alternate_solutions.idea: Both points are on $L$, so $PQ=|\Delta\mu|\cdot|\vec d|$; the foot's parameter comes from the projection formula $\mu=\frac{\overrightarrow{P_0A}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$.
solution: Take $P_0(1,-1,2)$ on $L$ with $\vec d=(1,-1,2)$, $|\vec d|^2=6$. The point at parameter $\mu$ is $P_0+\mu\vec d$.
Foot of the perpendicular from $A(1,2,2)$: $\mu_P=\frac{\overrightarrow{P_0A}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}=\frac{(0,3,0)\cdot(1,-1,2)}{6}=-\frac12$.
The point $(-1,1,-2)$ of the second line is on $L$ at $\mu_Q=-2$ ($P_0-2\vec d=(-1,1,-2)$), and it is the intersection since it lies on both lines (the second line at $\lambda=0$).
$PQ=|\mu_Q-\mu_P|\,|\vec d|=\frac32\sqrt6$, so $2(PQ)^2=2\cdot\frac94\cdot6=27$.

useful_results: Foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to the line $P_0+\mu\vec d$: $\mu=\frac{\overrightarrow{P_0A}\cdot\vec d}{|\vec d|^2}$ (no equation to solve).
Two points on one line at parameters $\mu_1,\mu_2$ are at distance $|\mu_1-\mu_2|\,|\vec d|$.

To intersect two lines, equate coordinates: three equations, two unknowns; consistency is the intersection test. Here the directions $(1,-1,2)$ and $(1,-1,1)$ are not parallel, so the lines meet at most once.

concepts: Direction cosines of a unit vector with given angles, and angle between vectors
questions.question: Let a unit vector which makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with $2\hat i+2\hat j-\hat k$ and an angle of $45^\circ$ with $\hat i-\hat k$ be $\vec C$. Then $\vec C+\left(-\frac12\hat i+\frac{1}{3\sqrt2}\hat j-\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\hat k\right)$ is:
questions.key_idea: The two angle conditions are linear in $(a,b,c)$ ($a-c=1$ and $2a+2b-c=\frac32$); with $a^2+b^2+c^2=1$ they leave a quadratic in $a$ with two roots.
solution: Let $\vec C=a\hat i+b\hat j+c\hat k$ with $a^2+b^2+c^2=1$ ...(3).
Angle $60^\circ$ with $2\hat i+2\hat j-\hat k$ (length $3$): $(a,b,c)\cdot(2,2,-1)=1\times3\times\frac12$, so $2a+2b-c=\frac32$ ...(1).
Angle $45^\circ$ with $\hat i-\hat k$ (length $\sqrt2$): $(a,b,c)\cdot(1,0,-1)=1\times\sqrt2\times\frac1{\sqrt2}$, so $a-c=1$ ...(2).
From (2) $c=a-1$; then (1) gives $a+2b=\frac12$, so $b=\frac{1-2a}{4}$.
Substituting into (3): $a^2+\left(\frac{1-2a}{4}\right)^2+(a-1)^2=1$, which simplifies to $36a^2-36a+1=0$.
$a=\frac{36\pm\sqrt{36^2-4\cdot36}}{72}=\frac12\pm\frac{\sqrt2}{3}$.
Then $b=\frac{1-2a}{4}=\mp\frac{1}{3\sqrt2}$ and $c=a-1=-\frac12\pm\frac{\sqrt2}{3}$ (upper signs together, lower signs together).
Add $-\frac12\hat i+\frac1{3\sqrt2}\hat j-\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\hat k$: upper signs give $\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{3},\,0,\,-\frac12\right)$.
Lower signs give $\left(-\frac{\sqrt2}{3},\,\frac{\sqrt2}{3},\,-\frac12-\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}\right)$, which is not among the options (option (4) has $+\frac12$).
So $\vec C+\left(\cdots\right)=\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\hat i-\frac12\hat k$, which is option (3).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's working is correct in substance but its last lines are mislabelled and incomplete: it names the root of the quadratic 'C' (it is the x-component a), writes b with a bare '-+' sign and only carries one of the two roots to the final vector without saying that the other root gives a vector not in the options. Added the sign pairing and the check of the second root; the final answer (3) is unchanged.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $\vec C=\vec C_0+s\vec e$, where $\vec C_0$ lies in the span of the two given directions and satisfies both angle conditions, and $\vec e=\vec n\times\vec m$ is perpendicular to both; then only $|\vec C|=1$ remains, a one-line equation for $s$.
solution: Let $\vec n=(2,2,-1)$, $\vec m=(1,0,-1)$. The conditions are $\vec C\cdot\vec n=\frac32$ and $\vec C\cdot\vec m=1$ (a line of solutions in space).

Seek $\vec C_0=x\vec n+y\vec m$: $\vec n\cdot\vec n=9$, $\vec n\cdot\vec m=3$, $\vec m\cdot\vec m=2$ give $9x+3y=\frac32$ and $3x+2y=1$, so $x=0$, $y=\frac12$ and $\vec C_0=\left(\frac12,0,-\frac12\right)$, $|\vec C_0|^2=\frac12$.
The solution line has direction $\vec e=\vec n\times\vec m=(-2,1,-2)$, $|\vec e|^2=9$, and $\vec C_0\perp\vec e$.
$|\vec C|^2=\frac12+9s^2=1$ gives $s=\pm\frac{\sqrt2}{6}$.
$\vec C=\left(\frac12\mp\frac{\sqrt2}{3},\ \pm\frac{\sqrt2}{6},\ -\frac12\mp\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\right)$.

For the lower sign, $s=-\frac{\sqrt2}{6}$, i.e. $\vec C=\left(\frac12+\frac{\sqrt2}{3},-\frac{\sqrt2}{6},-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\right)$, adding $\left(-\frac12,\frac{\sqrt2}{6},-\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\right)$ gives $\left(\frac{\sqrt2}{3},0,-\frac12\right)$, option (3); the upper sign gives $\left(-\frac{\sqrt2}{3},\frac{\sqrt2}{3},-\frac12-\frac{2\sqrt2}{3}\right)$, not an option.

useful_results: Angle conditions with fixed vectors are linear: $\vec C\cdot\vec u=|\vec u|\cos\theta$ (for unit $\vec C$). Two of them plus $|\vec C|=1$ give at most two vectors.

The set of solutions of two linear conditions is a line with direction $\vec n\times\vec m$; a point of it closest to the origin is $\vec C_0=x\vec n+y\vec m$, and $|\vec C|^2=|\vec C_0|^2+s^2|\vec e|^2$ (Pythagoras).
Number of such unit vectors is $2$, $1$ or $0$ according as $|\vec C_0|<1$, $=1$, $>1$: here $|\vec C_0|^2=\frac12<1$, giving two.
Check on the answer: $\vec C=\left(\frac12+\frac{\sqrt2}{3},-\frac{\sqrt2}{6},-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt2}{3}\right)$ has $\vec C\cdot(2,2,-1)=\frac32$ and $\vec C\cdot(1,0,-1)=1$.

concepts: Scalar triple product and unit vector along the sum of two vectors
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i+4\hat j-5\hat k$ and $\vec c=x\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$, $x\in\mathbb R$. If $\vec d$ is the unit vector in the direction of $\vec b+\vec c$ such that $\vec a\cdot\vec d=1$, then $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec c$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec d=\lambda(\vec b+\vec c)$ with $\lambda>0$; the two conditions $\vec a\cdot\vec d=1$ and $|\vec d|=1$ fix $x$.
solution: $\vec b+\vec c=(2+x)\hat i+6\hat j-2\hat k$, so $\vec d=\lambda\left((2+x)\hat i+6\hat j-2\hat k\right)$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec d=1$: $\lambda(x+6)=1$ ...(1).
So $\vec c=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$.
$\vec a\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&1&1\\2&4&-5\end{matrix}\right|=-9\hat i+7\hat j+2\hat k$.
$(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec c=-9+14+6=11$, which is option (1).

alternate_solutions.idea: A scalar triple product is a determinant, and it is linear in $x$ (the unknown sits in one row); no cross product is needed once $x$ is known.
solution: $x=1$ follows as before from $\vec a\cdot\vec d=1$ and $|\vec d|=1$.
$(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec c=\left|\begin{matrix}1&1&1\\2&4&-5\\x&2&3\end{matrix}\right|=1(12+10)-1(6+5x)+1(4-4x)=20-9x$.
At $x=1$ this is $11$, option (1).

useful_results: $(\vec a\times\vec b)\cdot\vec c=\det[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c]$; with $\vec c=(x,2,3)$ the value is $20-9x$, linear in $x$, which also shows how the answer depends on $x$.
$\vec a\cdot\hat s=|\vec a|\cos\theta$: when $\vec a\cdot\vec d=1$ and $|\vec a|=\sqrt3$, $\cos\theta=\frac1{\sqrt3}$.
For $\vec d=\frac{\vec s}{|\vec s|}$, $\vec a\cdot\vec d=1$ is equivalent to $(\vec a\cdot\vec s)^2=|\vec s|^2$ together with $\vec a\cdot\vec s>0$; here $(x+6)^2=(x+2)^2+40$ and $x+6>0$.

concepts: Cross product, perpendicularity and minimisation of a distance between vectors
questions.question: Consider three vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$. Let $|\vec a|=2$, $|\vec b|=3$ and $\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c$. If $\alpha\in\left[0,\frac\pi3\right]$ is the angle between the vectors $\vec b$ and $\vec c$, then the minimum value of $27|\vec c-\vec a|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c$ makes $\vec a\perp\vec c$, so $|\vec c-\vec a|^2=|\vec c|^2+4$ and $|\vec c|=\frac{2}{3\sin\alpha}$.
solution: $\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c$, so $\vec a\perp\vec b$ and $\vec a\perp\vec c$: $\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec c=0$.
$|\vec c-\vec a|^2=|\vec c|^2+|\vec a|^2-2\vec c\cdot\vec a=4+|\vec c|^2$.
$|\vec a|=|\vec b\times\vec c|=|\vec b||\vec c|\sin\alpha$, so $2=3|\vec c|\sin\alpha$ and $\sin\alpha\,|\vec c|=\frac23$.
$\sin^2\alpha=\frac{4}{9|\vec c|^2}$, so $|\vec c|^2=\frac{4}{9\sin^2\alpha}$.
$|\vec c-\vec a|^2=4+\frac{4}{9\sin^2\alpha}$.
This is smallest when $\sin\alpha$ is largest; on $\left(0,\frac\pi3\right]$ that is $\sin\alpha=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
$27|\vec c-\vec a|^2=27\left[4+\frac{4\cdot4}{9\cdot3}\right]=27\cdot\frac{124}{27}=124$, which is option (2).
useful_results: $\vec a=\vec b\times\vec c$ implies $\vec a\perp\vec b$, $\vec a\perp\vec c$ and $|\vec a|=|\vec b||\vec c|\sin\alpha$; the triple $\vec b,\vec c,\vec a$ is right-handed.
If $\vec u\perp\vec w$ then $|\vec u\pm\vec w|^2=|\vec u|^2+|\vec w|^2$ (Pythagoras).

$\sin\alpha$ increases on $\left[0,\frac\pi2\right]$, so a quantity of the form $\frac{k}{\sin^2\alpha}$ is minimised at the largest allowed $\alpha$; at $\alpha=0$ the cross product would vanish, so $\alpha\in\left(0,\frac\pi3\right]$ in fact.
Quick check at the minimum: $|\vec c|=\frac{2}{3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2}=\frac{4}{3\sqrt3}$, $|\vec c|^2=\frac{16}{27}$.

concepts: Dot product, magnitude and angle between vectors with a cross-product
questions.question: Let $\vec a=6\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$ and $\vec b=\hat i+\hat j$. If $\vec c$ is a vector such that $|\vec c|\ge6$, $\vec a\cdot\vec c=6|\vec c|$, $|\vec c-\vec a|=2\sqrt2$ and the angle between $\vec a\times\vec b$ and $\vec c$ is $60^\circ$, then $\left|(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c\right|$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Square $|\vec c-\vec a|=2\sqrt2$ and use $\vec a\cdot\vec c=6|\vec c|$ to get a quadratic in $|\vec c|$; the condition $|\vec c|\ge6$ picks the root.
solution: $|(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c|=|\vec a\times\vec b|\,|\vec c|\sin60^\circ=|\vec a\times\vec b|\,|\vec c|\,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
$\vec a\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\6&1&-1\\1&1&0\end{matrix}\right|=\hat i-\hat j+5\hat k$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|=\sqrt{27}$.
$|\vec c-\vec a|=2\sqrt2$ gives $|\vec c|^2+|\vec a|^2-2\vec a\cdot\vec c=8$, with $|\vec a|^2=36+1+1=38$.
Using $\vec a\cdot\vec c=6|\vec c|$: $|\vec c|^2+38-12|\vec c|=8$, so $|\vec c|^2-12|\vec c|+30=0$.
$|\vec c|=\frac{12\pm\sqrt{144-120}}{2}=6\pm\sqrt6$; since $|\vec c|\ge6$, $|\vec c|=6+\sqrt6$.
$|(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c|=\sqrt{27}\left(6+\sqrt6\right)\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\frac{9}{2}\left(6+\sqrt6\right)$, which is option (2).
useful_results: $|\vec u\times\vec w|=|\vec u||\vec w|\sin\theta$ for the angle $\theta$ between them; $|(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c|$ needs only $|\vec a\times\vec b|$, $|\vec c|$ and the given angle, not the direction of $\vec c$.
$|\vec c-\vec a|^2=|\vec c|^2+|\vec a|^2-2\vec a\cdot\vec c$: when $\vec a\cdot\vec c$ is a multiple of $|\vec c|$, the result is a quadratic in $|\vec c|$ alone.
$\sqrt{27}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\frac92$: write $|\vec a\times\vec b|$ as $3\sqrt3$ to simplify early.
Check: for $|\vec c|=6+\sqrt6$, $\vec a\cdot\vec c=6(6+\sqrt6)$ makes the angle between $\vec a$ and $\vec c$ satisfy $\cos\theta=\frac{6}{\sqrt{38}}$.

concepts: Direction cosines and distance of a point from a coordinate axis
questions.question: Let $P(x,y,z)$ be a point in the first octant, whose projection in the $xy$-plane is the point $Q$. Let $OP=\gamma$; the angle between $OQ$ and the positive $x$-axis is $\theta$; and the angle between $OP$ and the positive $z$-axis is $\phi$, where $O$ is the origin. Then the distance of $P$ from the $x$-axis is:
questions.key_idea: The distance from the $x$-axis is $\sqrt{\gamma^2-x^2}$, and $x=\gamma\sin\phi\cos\theta$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{OP}=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}=x\hat i+y\hat j$, with $|OP|=\gamma=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}$.
The angle between $OQ$ and the $x$-axis: $\cos\theta=\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}$, so $\cos^2\theta=\frac{x^2}{x^2+y^2}=\frac{x^2}{\gamma^2-z^2}$.
The angle between $OP$ and the $z$-axis: $\cos\phi=\frac{z}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}}=\frac z\gamma$, so $z^2=\gamma^2\cos^2\phi$ and $\gamma^2-z^2=\gamma^2\sin^2\phi$.
Therefore $\cos^2\theta=\frac{x^2}{\gamma^2\sin^2\phi}$, i.e. $x^2=\gamma^2\sin^2\phi\cos^2\theta$.
The distance of $P$ from the $x$-axis is $d=\sqrt{y^2+z^2}=\sqrt{\gamma^2-x^2}$.
$d=\sqrt{\gamma^2-\gamma^2\sin^2\phi\cos^2\theta}=\gamma\sqrt{1-\sin^2\phi\cos^2\theta}$, which is option (3).

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the direction cosine $l=\cos\psi$ of $OP$ with the $x$-axis: $d=OP\sin\psi$ and $\cos\psi=\sin\phi\cos\theta$ by spherical coordinates.
solution: Spherical coordinates: $P=\gamma(\sin\phi\cos\theta,\ \sin\phi\sin\theta,\ \cos\phi)$, since $OQ=\gamma\sin\phi$ and $z=\gamma\cos\phi$.
The direction cosine of $OP$ along the $x$-axis is $l=\sin\phi\cos\theta=\cos\psi$, where $\psi$ is the angle between $OP$ and the $x$-axis.
The distance of $P$ from the $x$-axis is $OP\sin\psi=\gamma\sqrt{1-\cos^2\psi}=\gamma\sqrt{1-\sin^2\phi\cos^2\theta}$: option (3).

useful_results: Spherical coordinates (colatitude $\phi$ from the $z$-axis, azimuth $\theta$ from the $x$-axis): $(x,y,z)=\gamma(\sin\phi\cos\theta,\sin\phi\sin\theta,\cos\phi)$.
Distance of $P(x,y,z)$ from the $x$-, $y$-, $z$-axis is $\sqrt{y^2+z^2}$, $\sqrt{x^2+z^2}$, $\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$; in terms of the direction cosine $l$ of $OP$ with an axis it is $\gamma\sqrt{1-l^2}$.
Direction cosines satisfy $l^2+m^2+n^2=1$.
Check: $\theta=0,\phi=\frac\pi2$ puts $P$ on the $x$-axis, and the formula gives $\gamma\sqrt{1-1}=0$.

concepts: Unit vector along a given vector and dot product with a vector
questions.question: Let $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$, $\vec b=2\hat i+3\hat j-5\hat k$ and $\vec c=3\hat i-\hat j+\lambda\hat k$ be three vectors. Let $\vec r$ be a unit vector along $\vec b+\vec c$. If $\vec r\cdot\vec a=3$, then $3\lambda$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\vec r=k(\vec b+\vec c)$ with $|\vec r|=1$ and $\vec r\cdot\vec a=3$ give two equations in $k,\lambda$; eliminating $k$ leaves a linear equation in $\lambda$.
solution: $\vec r=k(\vec b+\vec c)$ with $\vec b+\vec c=5\hat i+2\hat j+(\lambda-5)\hat k$.
$\vec r\cdot\vec a=k\left(\vec b\cdot\vec a+\vec c\cdot\vec a\right)=3$, with $\vec b\cdot\vec a=2+6-15$ and $\vec c\cdot\vec a=3-2+3\lambda$.
$|\vec r|=1$: $k\sqrt{25+4+(5-\lambda)^2}=k\sqrt{54+\lambda^2-10\lambda}$, so $k^2(54+\lambda^2-10\lambda)=1$ ...(2)
From (1), $k=\frac{3}{-6+3\lambda}=\frac{1}{\lambda-2}$.
Put in (2): $54+\lambda^2-10\lambda=(\lambda-2)^2=\lambda^2-4\lambda+4$.
$50=6\lambda$, so $\lambda=\frac{25}{3}$ and $3\lambda=25$, which is option (3).
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes 3 = k(-3 + 3*lambda) in equation (1); the sum is 2+6-15+3-2+3*lambda = -6 + 3*lambda (the PDF's very next line uses k = 3/(-6+3 lambda), so (1) is a typo). Corrected to k(-6+3 lambda); the answer 25 is unchanged.
useful_results: $\vec r\cdot\vec a$ is linear in the unknown scale factor $k$ for $\vec r=k\vec s$; $|\vec r|=1$ fixes $k=\pm\frac1{|\vec s|}$, so $\vec r\cdot\vec a=3$ becomes $\vec s\cdot\vec a=\pm3|\vec s|$.
Sign condition: $\vec r\cdot\vec a=3>0$ forces $\vec s\cdot\vec a=3\lambda-6>0$, so $\lambda>2$ (true for $\lambda=\frac{25}{3}$) and $k>0$.
Squaring $\vec s\cdot\vec a=3|\vec s|$ gives $(3\lambda-6)^2=9(\lambda^2-10\lambda+54)$, in which the $\lambda^2$ terms cancel: the quadratic collapses to a linear equation.
Check at $\lambda=\frac{25}3$: $\vec s\cdot\vec a=19$ and $|\vec s|^2=\frac{361}{9}$, so $\vec r\cdot\vec a=\frac{19}{19/3}=3$.

concepts: Area of a triangle using the cross product
questions.question: Let three vectors $\vec a=\alpha\hat i+4\hat j+2\hat k$, $\vec b=5\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k$, $\vec c=x\hat i+y\hat j+z\hat k$ form a triangle such that $\vec c=\vec a-\vec b$ and the area of the triangle is $5\sqrt6$. If $\alpha$ is a positive real number, then $|\vec c|^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: For a triangle with sides $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c=\vec a-\vec b$, the area is $\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b|$; this gives an equation in $\alpha$.
solution: $\vec c=\vec a-\vec b=(\alpha-5)\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k$.
Area of the triangle $=\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b|=5\sqrt6$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|=10\sqrt6$.
$\vec a\times\vec b=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\\alpha&4&2\\5&3&4\end{matrix}\right|=10\hat i-(4\alpha-10)\hat j+(3\alpha-20)\hat k$.
$25\alpha^2-200\alpha+600=600$, so $25\alpha(\alpha-8)=0$; since $\alpha>0$, $\alpha=8$.
$\vec c=3\hat i+\hat j-2\hat k$, so $|\vec c|^2=9+1+4=14$, which is option (1).

alternate_solutions.idea: Lagrange's identity $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$ gives the equation from dot products alone, with no determinant.
solution: $|\vec a|^2=\alpha^2+20$, $|\vec b|^2=25+9+16=50$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec b=5\alpha+12+8=5\alpha+20$.
$50\alpha^2+1000-25\alpha^2-200\alpha-400=600$, so $25\alpha^2-200\alpha=0$, giving $\alpha=8$ (as $\alpha>0$).

useful_results: A triangle with side vectors $\vec a,\vec b$ and $\vec c=\vec a-\vec b$ has area $\frac12|\vec a\times\vec b|$ (the same for any two of the sides, since $\vec a\times\vec c=\vec a\times(\vec a-\vec b)=-\vec a\times\vec b$).
Lagrange's identity: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec b|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec b)^2$; the $\alpha^4$-type terms cancel so the equation is quadratic.
Check: $\alpha=8$ gives $\vec a=(8,4,2)$, $\vec a\times\vec b=(10,-22,4)\cdot$ with magnitude $\sqrt{100+484+16}=\sqrt{600}=10\sqrt6$.

concepts: Cross product equation $\vec a\times\vec r=\vec a\times\vec b$ and an inequality in the angles of a triangle
questions.question:
Between the following two statements:
Statement I: Let $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j-3\hat k$ and $\vec b=2\hat i+\hat j-\hat k$. Then the vector $\vec r$ satisfying $\vec a\times\vec r=\vec a\times\vec b$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec r=0$ is of magnitude $\sqrt{10}$.
Statement II: In a triangle $ABC$, $\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C\ge-\frac32$.
options: Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
questions.answer: (2) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.
questions.key_idea: Lagrange's identity with $\vec a\cdot\vec r=0$ gives $|\vec a\times\vec b|=|\vec a||\vec r|$; for Statement II take the circumcentre $O$ and use $|\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{OC}|^2\ge0$.
solution: For any two vectors, $|\vec c\times\vec d|^2=|\vec c|^2|\vec d|^2-(\vec c\cdot\vec d)^2$; replace $\vec c=\vec a$, $\vec d=\vec r$: $|\vec a\times\vec r|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec r|^2-(\vec a\cdot\vec r)^2$.
Since $\vec a\times\vec r=\vec a\times\vec b$ and $\vec a\cdot\vec r=0$: $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=|\vec a|^2|\vec r|^2$.
$\vec a\times\vec b=(1,-5,-3)$ so $|\vec a\times\vec b|^2=35$, and $|\vec a|^2=14$.
$35=14|\vec r|^2$, so $|\vec r|=\sqrt{\frac{35}{14}}=\sqrt{\frac52}\ne\sqrt{10}$. Statement I is incorrect.
Statement II: let $O$ be the circumcentre, with $|\overrightarrow{OA}|=|\overrightarrow{OB}|=|\overrightarrow{OC}|=R$ ...(2).
$\left|\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{OC}\right|^2\ge0$ ...(1).
Expanding with (2): $3R^2+2\left(\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{OB}\cdot\overrightarrow{OC}+\overrightarrow{OC}\cdot\overrightarrow{OA}\right)\ge0$.

The angle between $\overrightarrow{OA}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}$ is $2C$ (central angle), and so on, so each dot product is $R^2\cos2C,\ R^2\cos2A,\ R^2\cos2B$: $3R^2+2R^2(\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C)\ge0$.
So $\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C\ge-\frac32$. Statement II is correct: option (2).

alternate_solutions.idea: Statement I: solve $\vec a\times(\vec r-\vec b)=\vec 0$ directly, $\vec r=\vec b+t\vec a$. Statement II: use $\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C=-1-4\cos A\cos B\cos C$ and bound the product by $\frac18$.
solution: Statement I: $\vec a\times(\vec r-\vec b)=\vec0$ means $\vec r-\vec b=t\vec a$, i.e. $\vec r=\vec b+t\vec a$.
$\vec a\cdot\vec r=0$ gives $\vec a\cdot\vec b+t|\vec a|^2=0$: $7+14t=0$, so $t=-\frac12$.
$\vec r=\vec b-\frac12\vec a=\left(\frac32,0,\frac12\right)$, $|\vec r|^2=\frac94+\frac14=\frac52\ne10$: Statement I is incorrect.
Statement II: in a triangle $\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C=-1-4\cos A\cos B\cos C$ (e.g. equilateral: $-\frac32=-1-4\cdot\frac18$).
So the claim is $\cos A\cos B\cos C\le\frac18$. If $\cos C<0$ then $A,B$ are acute and the product is negative.
If $\cos C\ge0$: $\cos A\cos B=\frac12[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)]\le\frac12(1-\cos C)$, so the product is $\le\frac12\cos C(1-\cos C)\le\frac18$ (maximum of $c(1-c)$ is $\frac14$ at $c=\frac12$).
Hence the inequality holds for every triangle: Statement II is correct; option (2).

useful_results: Lagrange's identity: $|\vec c\times\vec d|^2=|\vec c|^2|\vec d|^2-(\vec c\cdot\vec d)^2$.

$\vec a\times\vec r=\vec a\times\vec b\iff\vec r=\vec b+t\vec a$ (all $\vec r$ differ from $\vec b$ by a multiple of $\vec a$); adding $\vec a\cdot\vec r=k$ fixes $t=\frac{k-\vec a\cdot\vec b}{|\vec a|^2}$, giving a unique $\vec r$.
In a triangle: $\cos2A+\cos2B+\cos2C=-1-4\cos A\cos B\cos C$, which is at least $-\frac32$, with equality for the equilateral triangle; also $\cos A+\cos B+\cos C\le\frac32$.
Technique: to prove an inequality in $A,B,C$, put the circumcentre at the origin and expand a sum of unit-vector squares $\ge0$.

concepts: Area of a parallelogram with given diagonals; integer solutions
questions.question: Let $\vec a=2\hat i+\alpha\hat j+\hat k$, $\vec b=-\hat i+\hat k$, $\vec c=\beta\hat j-\hat k$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are integers and $\alpha\beta=-6$. Let the values of the ordered pair $(\alpha,\beta)$, for which the area of the parallelogram of diagonals $\vec a+\vec b$ and $\vec b+\vec c$ is $\frac{\sqrt{21}}{2}$, be $(\alpha_1,\beta_1)$ and $(\alpha_2,\beta_2)$. Then $\alpha_1^2+\beta_1^2-\alpha_2\beta_2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Area of a parallelogram with diagonals $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ is $\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$; with $\alpha\beta=-6$ this gives $\alpha^2+5\beta^2=29$.
solution: Area of the parallelogram with diagonals $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ is $\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|=\frac{\sqrt{21}}{2}$, with $\vec d_1=\vec a+\vec b=\hat i+\alpha\hat j+2\hat k$ and $\vec d_2=\vec b+\vec c=-\hat i+\beta\hat j$.
$\vec d_1\times\vec d_2=\left|\begin{matrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\1&\alpha&2\\-1&\beta&0\end{matrix}\right|=-2\beta\hat i-2\hat j+(\alpha+\beta)\hat k$.
$\sqrt{4\beta^2+4+(\alpha+\beta)^2}=\sqrt{21}$, so $4\beta^2+4+\alpha^2+\beta^2+2\alpha\beta=21$, i.e. $\alpha^2+5\beta^2+2\alpha\beta=17$.
With $\alpha\beta=-6$: $\alpha^2+5\beta^2-12=17$, so $\alpha^2+5\beta^2=29$.
For integers with $\alpha\beta=-6$: $(\alpha,\beta)=(-3,2)$ gives $9+20=29$ and $(3,-2)$ gives $9+20=29$; the other integer pairs (for example $(6,-1)$: $41$; $(2,-3)$: $49$) fail.
$\alpha_1^2+\beta_1^2-\alpha_2\beta_2=9+4-(3)(-2)=9+4+6=19$, which is option (3).

alternate_solutions.idea: Lagrange's identity $|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|^2=|\vec d_1|^2|\vec d_2|^2-(\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2)^2$ uses $\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2=-1+\alpha\beta=-7$ directly, with no determinant.
solution: $|\vec d_1|^2=\alpha^2+5$, $|\vec d_2|^2=\beta^2+1$ and $\vec d_1\cdot\vec d_2=-1+\alpha\beta=-7$.
$|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|^2=21$ gives $(\alpha^2+5)(\beta^2+1)-49=21$.
$\alpha^2\beta^2+\alpha^2+5\beta^2+5=70$; with $\alpha^2\beta^2=36$ this gives $\alpha^2+5\beta^2=29$.

The integer pairs with $\alpha\beta=-6$ are $(\pm1,\mp6),(\pm2,\mp3),(\pm3,\mp2),(\pm6,\mp1)$, and only $(\pm3,\mp2)$ gives $29$: the same pairs as before, and $\alpha_1^2+\beta_1^2-\alpha_2\beta_2=13+6=19$.

useful_results: Parallelogram with diagonals $\vec d_1,\vec d_2$ has area $\frac12|\vec d_1\times\vec d_2|$ (the sides are $\frac{\vec d_1\pm\vec d_2}{2}$); with sides $\vec u,\vec v$ the area is $|\vec u\times\vec v|$.
Lagrange's identity turns a cross-product magnitude into dot products, so a given product such as $\alpha\beta$ can be used immediately.
For an integer pair with product $-6$, list the divisor pairs ($4$ unordered, $8$ ordered) and test the second equation; a sum of squares with weights ($\alpha^2+5\beta^2$) quickly rules out most.
Since $\alpha_2\beta_2=-6$ for either pair, the requested expression equals $\alpha_1^2+\beta_1^2+6=13+6$.
